articles.title: Senate Republicans shift $69B in defense reconciliation funding to regular appropriations
articles.description: Senate Republicans are proposing to move nearly $69 billion in defense funding sought by the Trump administration through budget reconciliation into the regular appropriations process as part of a nearly $1.1 trillion fiscal year 2027 defense spending bill that makes major investments in munitions production, missile defense, drones, shipbuilding and military modernization. The Senate Appropriations Committee's Republican majority is providing the money as discretionary rather than the one-time mandatory spending originally requested by the administration. The committee argues that the approach would provide more stable, predictable funding for critical military capabilities, according to an explanatory statement released with the bill. The proposal reflects growing skepticism among Senate appropriators about the White House's plan to secure $350 billion in additional defense funding through reconciliation. Appropriations Chairwoman Susan Collins (R-ME) and other Republicans have questioned the cost and scope of another party-line package, while some defense hawks, including Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman Roger Wicker (R-MS), continue to press for the full request. Though Senate Republicans have not formally abandoned the reconciliation effort, the appropriations proposal would shift a substantial portion of the administration's priorities into the regular spending process. Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA), the committee's top Democrat and likely chairwoman next year when her party takes the majority, said she objects to the proposal. “This bill delivers a truly massive windfall for Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon -- meeting President Trump’s eye-popping request -- while doing next to nothing to rein in this president who is waging illegal wars,” she said. “We cannot and should not accept the roadmap Senate Republicans have laid out which would hurl hundreds of billions of dollars more at the Pentagon while doing exceptionally little to help families get by.” Munitions and missile defense The committee's proposal includes $47.2 billion for additional munitions procurement and acceleration efforts, $35.6 billion for air and missile defense capabilities and $6.2 billion for drone and counter-drone programs. The bill provides $40.6 billion for new multiyear procurement contracts covering nine munitions: Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles, Guided Multiple Launch Rocket Systems, Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors, Precision Strike Missiles Increment 1, Standard Missile-3 Block IB and Block IIA, Standard Missile-6, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense missiles and Tomahawk cruise missiles. The proposal also includes $1.5 billion for additional quantities of Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles and Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile-Extended Range missiles under existing multiyear procurement agreements. Another $1 billion would procure additional Joint Advanced Tactical Missiles, while $1.9 billion would support systems made by new industry entrants, including Blackbeard Ground Launch, the Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector, the Family of Affordable Mass Missile, low-cost cruise missiles and containerized munitions. An additional $1.4 billion would replenish inventories of weapons including Joint Air-to-Ground Missiles, Evolved Sea Sparrow Missiles, Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System rockets, 30mm proximity ammunition, Joint Direct Attack Munitions and general-purpose bombs. For air and missile defense, the committee provides $35.6 billion, including $32 billion for additional defensive interceptors, $812 million for two additional THAAD radars and $170 million for air and missile defense software development and integration. The proposal separately includes $9.4 billion in discretionary funding for Golden Dome initiatives, which the administration had requested as mandatory spending. The investment is intended to advance protection of critical infrastructure in the United States and its territories against ballistic, hypersonic and cruise missiles, as well as other advanced aerial threats. The White House, however, has requested $17.5 billion for Golden Dome in FY-27. F-35 and drone investments The committee provides $11.1 billion for Joint Strike Fighter procurement, modifications and sustainment, along with $2.9 billion for research, development, test and evaluation. The funding includes $5.7 billion originally requested as mandatory spending. The bill adds $2.4 billion for 15 additional F-35Cs, $1 billion for five additional F-35Bs and $704 million for five additional F-35As. For drones and counter-drone capabilities, the committee provides $6.2 billion for research, development and procurement. That includes $3 billion in additional discretionary funding for the Defense Autonomous Working Group. The administration, meanwhile, was seeking almost $55 billion for DAWG in FY-27 in the hopes of establishing a new combatant command. Shipbuilding and industrial base The bill provides $42 billion for shipbuilding, including $1.9 billion for a second DDG-51 destroyer. The committee provides $329 million for the Submarine Industrial Base program and $595 million for the Surface Ship Industrial Base program to improve supply chain resilience. The proposal includes incremental funding for one Columbia-class submarine, two Virginia-class submarines, one aircraft carrier refueling and complex overhaul, one FF(X) frigate, one LPD Flight II amphibious transport dock and one LHA replacement ship. Service-specific investments and space The Army would receive $61.3 billion for procurement and $19.4 billion for research and development, including $360 million for CH-47s, $185 million for the Improved Turbine Engine Program and $2.1 billion for Future Long-Range Assault Aircraft modernization. The Navy would receive $113.4 billion for procurement and $29.9 billion for research and development, including $250 million for the Sea-Launched Cruise Missile-Nuclear, $350 million for sonobuoys and additional funding for ship missile defenses, Coyote systems and patrol boats. The Air Force would receive $78.9 billion for procurement and $67.4 billion for research and development. Major additions include $1.4 billion for eight C-130Js for the Air National Guard, funding for F-15EX enhancements and $150 million for Next Generation Adaptive Propulsion. The proposal also supports the administration's $4.5 billion Sentinel request. The Space Force would receive $13.8 billion for procurement and $32.3 billion for research and development, including $3.3 billion for the Space Data Network, $2 billion for space-based moving target indicator capability and $7.1 billion for 54 National Security Space Launch missions. Security cooperation would receive $5.4 billion, including $1 billion for partnerships with Taiwan and the Philippines, $750 million for Ukraine and $175 million for the Baltic states. The bill provides another $500 million for U.S.-Israeli missile defense cooperation, plus funding for counter-drone and emerging technology cooperation and subterranean operations.
